items.stem: The magnetic field outside a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that of
items.answer: a bar magnet
items.markingKey: Solenoid field resembles a bar magnet with N and S ends.

items.stem: A circuit diagram shows a circle with a cross. Which component does this symbol represent?
items.answer: a lamp
items.markingKey: A lamp is drawn as a circle with a cross.

items.stem: A village is supplied through a long cable. The resistance of the cables is multiplied by 5 while the current in the cables stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the power lost in the cables changes.
items.answer: The power lost in the cables becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power lost in the cables ∝ resistance of the cables; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Describe the electric field pattern for two positive charges close together, and state the direction of the force on an electron placed in the field.
items.answer: Lines curve away from both charges with a neutral point midway. Force on an electron: opposite to the field lines.
items.markingKey: 2 marks pattern with direction; 1 mark force direction.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but signals of much shorter wavelength often cannot. (b) Explain why the wavefronts get closer together when water waves move into a shallow region.
items.answer: (a) Long-wave radio has wavelengths comparable to the size of hills, so it diffracts around them; short wavelengths diffract very little. (b) The waves slow down but the frequency stays the same, so λ = v/f decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diffraction around obstacles; 1 mark: long λ diffracts more. (b) 1 mark: speed decreases; 1 mark: f constant so λ decreases.

items.stem: A X-ray signal has a frequency of 7.5 × 10¹⁷ Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum (speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
Answer both parts. (a) The Sun is (b) The Milky Way is
items.answer: (a) a medium-sized star (b) a galaxy containing billions of stars
items.markingKey: (a) The Sun is a typical main-sequence star of medium size. (b) Our galaxy has 100–400 billion stars.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The four outer planets are mainly (b) As a comet approaches the Sun, its speed
items.answer: (a) large and made of gas (b) increases
items.markingKey: (a) Inner planets: small and rocky; outer: gas giants (formed further from the Sun where volatile substances condensed). (b) Gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy as it falls closer.

items.stem: A student says current is "used up" by a lamp. Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: The same current flows in and out of the lamp; energy, not charge, is transferred in the lamp.

items.stem: A scrap-yard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars. Explain why aluminium is not attracted.
items.answer: Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the moderator is needed in a thermal fission reactor. (b) Explain where the energy released in fission comes from.
items.answer: (a) It slows down the fast neutrons released, because slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission. (b) The total mass of the products is slightly less than the original nucleus plus neutron; the lost mass is released as energy.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 600; paper 595; 3 mm aluminium 24; 2 cm lead 180. Background is 20 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: Which change would make a d.c. motor turn faster?
options: Increasing the number of turns on the coil
items.answer: Increasing the number of turns on the coil
items.markingKey: Speed increases with more turns, larger current or a stronger field.

items.stem: A circuit diagram shows a triangle pointing at a bar. Which component does this symbol represent?
items.answer: a diode
items.markingKey: A diode is drawn as a triangle pointing at a bar.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the output of an a.c. generator reverses direction every half turn. (b) Compare the a.c. generator and the d.c. motor in terms of energy changes.
items.answer: (a) Each side of the coil moves up then down through the field, so the direction of cutting reverses. (b) Generator: kinetic → electrical; motor: electrical → kinetic.

items.stem: Two identical metal spheres on insulating stands carry charges of +12 nC and −6 nC. They touch briefly and are separated. Calculate the final charge on each and explain.
items.answer: 3.00 nC each: electrons move until charge is shared equally between identical spheres; total charge is conserved.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark shared equally; 1 mark conservation.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same ripple tank at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 5 Hz and wave Q has frequency 25 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave P (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: A microwave signal has a frequency of 6.0 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum (speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
The Sun mainly emits radiation in which regions of the spectrum?
items.answer: Infrared, visible and ultraviolet
items.markingKey: Most energy is in the IR, visible and UV regions.

items.stem: Explain why the strength of the Sun’s gravitational field decreases with distance and how this affects orbital speed.
items.answer: The field spreads out over a larger area further away; planets further away need less speed to stay in orbit, so they move more slowly.

items.stem: The p.d. across a lamp is 2.50 V and the current is 0.500 A. Calculate its resistance.

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets. (b) A chain of iron paper clips hangs from a magnet. Explain what happens when the magnet is removed if the clips are soft iron, and if they are steel.
items.answer: (a) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current. (b) Soft iron clips lose their induced magnetism and fall apart; steel clips keep some magnetism and may stay together.

items.stem: In a reactor, each fission releases on average 2.5 neutrons. Explain what fraction of these must, on average, go on to cause another fission for steady power, and how the coolant affects the reactor.
items.answer: Exactly one neutron per fission must cause another (the rest are absorbed or escape). Control rods absorb neutrons to set this rate; the moderator slows neutrons so they cause fission; the coolant removes heat to the boiler.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one per fission; 1 mark: role of named component.

items.stem: Sr-90 (proton number 38) decays by beta emission to form Y. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Y.
items.answer: Y: nucleon number 90, proton number 39. Sr-90 (Z = 38) → Y-90 (Z = 39) + β (e, Z = −1)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 90; 1 mark proton number 39; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a current-carrying wire placed between the poles of a magnet experiences a force. (b) A beam of electrons passes through a magnetic field at right angles. Explain why its path curves.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current interacts with the field of the magnet; the fields combine to be stronger on one side and weaker on the other, pushing the wire. (b) Moving charges are a current, so each electron feels a force at right angles to its velocity and to the field; this continually changes its direction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: field around wire; 1 mark: interaction gives force. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: A 1500 W metal-cased hair dryer is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin.
items.answer: A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire.

items.stem: A transformer powers a model railway. The number of primary turns is increased by 50% while the number of secondary turns stays the same. State and explain how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage falls to two thirds.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of primary turns^-1.00; factor = 1.50^-1.00 = 0.667. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth and becomes negatively charged with a charge of magnitude 6.4 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) State the charge on the cloth. (b) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it.
items.answer: (a) +6.4 × 10⁻⁹ C (equal and opposite) (b) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion.

items.stem: Plane water waves strike a straight barrier. The wavefronts make an angle of 40° with the barrier. State the angle of incidence (from the normal) and the angle that the reflected wavefronts make with the barrier.
items.answer: Angle of incidence = 40°; reflected wavefronts also make 40° with the barrier.
items.markingKey: The angle between wavefront and barrier equals the angle between ray and normal, so i = 40° [1]; i = r so reflected wavefronts at 40° [1].

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why satellite phones use microwaves rather than long-wave radio. (b) Explain two advantages of sending a signal digitally rather than as an analogue signal.
items.answer: (a) Microwaves pass through the ionosphere to reach the satellite; long-wave radio is reflected by the ionosphere. (b) Noise can be removed when digital signals are regenerated, so quality stays high; more data can be sent per second and data can be compressed or encrypted.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark each for two: regeneration removes noise; higher transmission rate; easily processed/stored by computers.

items.stem: the Crab Nebula is a supernova remnant containing a neutron star. State the stage of its life cycle it has reached and predict what will happen to it next, giving a reason.
items.answer: Supernova remnant containing a neutron star; next: the neutron star cools, because its fate depends on its mass.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stage; 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (mass).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the inner planets are rocky while the outer planets are gas giants. (b) Explain why a comet’s speed changes during its elliptical orbit.
items.answer: (a) Near the young Sun it was too hot for volatile substances to condense, so only rock and metal formed planets; further out, gases and ices could gather into giant planets. (b) Close to the Sun the gravitational pull is stronger and it gains kinetic energy as it falls in; it slows as it moves away.

items.stem: An appliance draws 5.00 A from a 240 V supply. Calculate its power.

A nucleus of strontium (Sr) has nucleon number 90 and proton number 38. (a) State the number of electrons in a neutral atom. (b) Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties. (c) State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
items.answer: (a) 38 (b) Same number of protons and electrons; chemistry depends on electrons. (c) proton +1, 1; neutron 0, 1; electron −1, about 1/1840

items.stem: A factory uses a radioactive source and detector to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil. (a) State which type of radiation is suitable and explain why. (b) Explain why the half-life of the source matters for this use. (c) Describe two safety precautions for workers.
items.answer: (a) Depends on penetration: alpha for short-range ionisation, beta for thin sheet thickness, gamma to pass through the body or packaging. (b) Long half-life for steady count over years; short half-life for medical use so the dose to the patient is low. (c) Shielding (lead), handling with tongs/remote, minimise time, maximise distance, wear dosimeter badge (any two).

items.stem: A wire is placed between the poles of a U-shaped magnet and connected to a power supply through a switch. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State the rule used to predict the direction of the force and what each finger represents. (c) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (d) Describe the effect of replacing the d.c. supply with an a.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion. (c) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (d) The force reverses direction many times a second, so the object vibrates (as in a loudspeaker).

items.stem: A 24 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors. (a) Calculate the total resistance of the circuit. (b) Calculate the p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor. (c) Calculate the current in the 3 Ω resistor. (d) Calculate the power dissipated in the whole circuit.

A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter, then pulls it out. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (c) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (c) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed.

items.stem: A sonar transmitter produces sound of frequency 1.50 kHz in sea water, where sound travels at 1480 m/s. Calculate the wavelength in cm.
items.markingKey: f = 1.50 × 10³ Hz; λ = v/f = 1480/1500 = 0.987 m = 98.7 cm. Unit conversion kHz → Hz is the usual error.

items.stem: A report describes how microwaves are used for satellite television and mobile phones. (a) A typical frequency used is 6.0 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength. (b) Explain why this radiation is suitable for this use. (c) Compare this radiation with gamma rays, used for treating cancer (radiotherapy), in terms of wavelength and frequency. (d) Describe one harmful effect of this radiation and one precaution.
items.answer: (a) 5.0 × 10⁻² m (b) They pass through the atmosphere and can be focused into narrow beams. (c) microwaves has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than gamma rays. (d) internal heating of body cells; limit exposure time/use shielding.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = c/f [2] (b) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Light from a distant galaxy shows a redshift that corresponds to a recession speed of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Explain what is meant by redshift. (b) Convert the distance to light-years (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m). (c) Explain how redshift data support the Big Bang theory. (d) State one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang.
items.answer: (a) An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a receding source. (b) 3.2 × 10⁸ light-years (c) More distant galaxies recede faster, so the Universe is expanding from an initial point. (d) Cosmic microwave background radiation.

items.stem: Mercury orbits the Sun at an average distance of 5.80 × 10¹⁰ m with a period of 88 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.7 N/kg. (a) Explain why planets further from the Sun have longer orbital periods. (b) Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Mercury.
items.answer: (a) They travel a longer distance per orbit and move more slowly because the Sun’s gravitational field is weaker there. (b) 193 s

items.stem: A 6 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 30 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the device when working.

A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 720; paper 715; 3 mm aluminium 432; 2 cm lead 19. Background is 18 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium stays above background, so gamma is present.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: Elena is designing a simple door lock that uses an electromagnet to hold a steel bolt. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (c) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (c) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls.

items.stem: Leila is studying the isotope strontium-90 (Z = 38). (a) State the number of neutrons in the nucleus. (b) State the number of electrons in a neutral atom. (c) Another isotope of strontium has two more neutrons. State its nucleon number and proton number. (d) State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
items.answer: (a) 52 (b) 38 (c) 92; 38 (d) proton +1, 1; neutron 0, 1; electron −1, about 1/1840

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 1200 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. Calculate its activity after 18 hours.
items.answer: 150 Bq

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 150 turns and carries 1.0 A; electromagnet Y has 200 turns and carries 2.0 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: Y – strength depends on turns × current (150 for X, 400 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: A potential divider has R₁ = 10 kΩ and R₂ = 20 kΩ in series across a 6 V supply. Calculate the output p.d. across R₂.

A transformer has 500 primary turns and 8000 secondary turns. The primary is connected to a 25,000 V a.c. supply. (a) State whether it is a step-up or step-down transformer. (b) Explain why the transformer would not work with a d.c. supply. (c) Explain why the core is made of soft iron.
items.answer: (a) step-up (b) A steady current gives a constant field; no change in field so no e.m.f. induced. (c) It is easily magnetised and demagnetised, concentrating the changing field to link both coils.

items.stem: Describe the electric field pattern for an isolated negative point charge, and state the direction of the force on an electron placed in the field.
items.answer: Radial lines pointing inwards. Force on an electron: opposite to the field lines.
items.markingKey: 2 marks pattern with direction; 1 mark force direction.

items.stem: In a ripple tank the water waves have wavelength 3.50 cm in the deep part. The dipper vibrates at 6 Hz. Over a shallow region the waves move at 0.105 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why. (c) The waves then pass through a gap 1.75 cm wide. Describe the diffraction pattern.
items.answer: (a) 0.210 m/s (b) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down. (c) Strong spreading into semicircular wavefronts (gap ≈ λ).
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 6 × 0.0350 = 0.210 m/s [2] (b) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2] (c) 1 mark pattern linked to gap/λ; 1 mark wavelength unchanged [2]

items.stem: A report describes how infrared are used for remote controls for televisions. (a) State the speed of this radiation in a vacuum. (b) A typical frequency used is 4.5 × 10¹³ Hz. Calculate its wavelength. (c) Explain why this radiation is suitable for this use. (d) Compare this radiation with gamma rays, used for treating cancer (radiotherapy), in terms of wavelength and frequency.
items.answer: (a) 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (b) 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ m (c) Low energy and short range, easily produced by an LED. (d) infrared has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than gamma rays.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) λ = c/f [2] (c) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (d) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Why do fusion reactions need extremely high temperatures?
options: Nuclei must move fast enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them
items.answer: Nuclei must move fast enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them
items.markingKey: Both nuclei are positive and repel.

items.stem: What happens to a d.c. motor if the current direction is reversed?
options: It turns faster in the same direction
items.answer: It turns the opposite way

items.stem: Explain why the output p.d. of a potential divider is shared in the ratio of the resistances.
items.answer: The same current flows through both resistors, so V = IR is proportional to R.

items.stem: A transformer has 400 turns on the primary and 40000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 240 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 24,000 V; step-up

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the electric field between two parallel plates, one positive and one negative. (b) Explain how an electrostatic paint sprayer gives an even coat and wastes less paint.
items.answer: (a) Uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from the positive plate to the negative plate (curving slightly at the edges). (b) Paint droplets are given the same charge, so they repel and spread out; the object is given the opposite charge (or earthed) so droplets are attracted to it, even round the back.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: parallel equally spaced; 1 mark: + to −. (b) 1 mark: droplets repel → even spray; 1 mark: attracted to object → less waste.

items.stem: A scrap-yard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars. State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger.
items.answer: More turns; larger current (or soft-iron core).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What causes day and night on Earth? (b) Why do we see phases of the Moon?
items.answer: (a) The Earth rotating on its axis once every 24 hours (b) Different amounts of the Moon’s sunlit half are visible from Earth as it orbits
items.markingKey: (a) Rotation (spin) about the axis; orbit takes a year. (b) The Moon reflects sunlight; its orbit changes how much of the lit side faces us.

items.stem: For a metal wire at constant temperature, the current–voltage graph is
options: a straight line through the origin
zero until 0.7 V then rising steeply
items.answer: a straight line through the origin
items.markingKey: Ohmic conductor: I ∝ V at constant temperature.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how alpha, beta and gamma radiation are deflected differently in an electric field. (b) Explain why a Geiger counter detects alpha particles only if it is very close to the source.
items.answer: (a) α (positive) deflects towards the negative plate, β (negative) deflects more strongly towards the positive plate as it is much lighter, γ is undeflected (no charge). (b) Alpha particles travel only a few cm in air before losing their energy.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each for α, β, γ. (b) [2]

items.stem: Plane water waves strike a straight barrier. The wavefronts make an angle of 25° with the barrier. State the angle of incidence (from the normal) and the angle that the reflected wavefronts make with the barrier.
items.answer: Angle of incidence = 25°; reflected wavefronts also make 25° with the barrier.
items.markingKey: The angle between wavefront and barrier equals the angle between ray and normal, so i = 25° [1]; i = r so reflected wavefronts at 25° [1].

items.stem: State two properties that visible light and gamma rays have in common, and one way in which they differ.
items.answer: Both are transverse, travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and can travel through a vacuum (any two). They differ in wavelength/frequency (and energy).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two shared properties (transverse; same speed in vacuum; no medium needed; can be reflected/refracted); 1 mark: different wavelength/frequency.

items.stem: An object is 1.6 × 10⁵ light-years away. Calculate its distance in km (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹² km) and explain what we are seeing when we look at it.
items.answer: 1.5 × 10¹⁸ km; light that left it 1.6 × 10⁵ years ago.
items.markingKey: 2 marks distance; 1 mark looking back in time.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What did this show? (b) A very small number of alpha particles bounced back. What did this show?
items.answer: (a) Most of the atom is empty space (b) The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
items.markingKey: (a) Most α passed through undeflected → atom mostly empty space. (b) Large deflections need a concentrated positive charge and mass.

items.stem: A beam of alpha particles and a beam of electrons enter the same magnetic field. Their deflections are
items.answer: in opposite directions

items.stem: Explain how the symbol for an LED differs from a diode and why.
items.answer: It has arrows pointing away showing that it emits light when current flows.

items.stem: A power station sends 1.0 × 10⁷ W along cables of total resistance 8 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 11,000 V and at 275,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 11,000 V: I = 909 A, loss = 6.61 × 10⁶ W. At 275,000 V: I = 36.4 A, loss = 1.06 × 10⁴ W. Raising V by ×25.0 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×625).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a metal rod held in the hand cannot be charged by rubbing, but a plastic rod can. (b) A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Explain why.
items.answer: (a) Metal is a conductor, so any charge flows away through the hand to earth; plastic is an insulator so charge stays where it is. (b) The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface positively charged by induction; unlike charges attract.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: charge induced in wall; 1 mark: attraction of unlike charges.

items.stem: On a field diagram, point P has field lines 2 times closer together than point Z. State what this tells you about the field and suggest where each point might be on a bar magnet.
items.answer: The field is stronger where lines are closer; the first point is nearer a pole, the second further away (or near the middle/side).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: closer lines = stronger field; 1 mark: sensible positions.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which list shows planets in order from the Sun? (b) The four outer planets are mainly
items.answer: (a) Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter (b) large and made of gas
items.markingKey: (a) Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. (b) Inner planets: small and rocky; outer: gas giants (formed further from the Sun where volatile substances condensed).

items.stem: Explain why a voltmeter must have a very high resistance.
items.answer: It is connected in parallel and should take almost no current, so it does not change the circuit.

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 1600 Bq. Its half-life is 12 days. Calculate its activity after 60 days.

Two waves travel along the same stretched spring at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 2 Hz and wave Q has frequency 5 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave P (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: A radio signal has a frequency of 7.5 × 10⁵ Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum (speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
Galaxy data (distance / million light-years; recession speed / m/s): E: 400, 8.8 × 10⁶; C: 200, 4.4 × 10⁶; A: 50, 1.1 × 10⁶. Describe the relationship and explain what it suggests about the Universe.
items.answer: Speed is (roughly) directly proportional to distance: further galaxies recede faster. This suggests the Universe is expanding, consistent with the Big Bang.
items.markingKey: 1 mark proportional/positive correlation; 1 mark expansion; 1 mark Big Bang link.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion. (b) Explain why fission products are dangerous.
items.answer: (a) Both release large amounts of energy from the nucleus (mass converted). Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei. (b) The daughter nuclei are radioactive and some have long half-lives, so waste must be stored safely for a long time.

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 150 turns and carries 2.0 A; electromagnet Y has 200 turns and carries 0.5 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: X – strength depends on turns × current (300 for X, 100 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why sockets in a ring main are connected in parallel. (b) Explain why adding another resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance of a circuit.
items.answer: (a) Each appliance gets the full mains p.d. and can be switched on or off independently. (b) It provides an extra path for charge, so more current flows for the same p.d.; R = V/I is smaller.

items.stem: A magnet is dropped through a vertical coil connected to a data logger. (a) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (b) Describe what the meter shows when the magnet is held still inside the coil.
items.answer: (a) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (b) Zero: no change in field, no e.m.f.

items.stem: Classify these materials as conductors or insulators and explain the difference in terms of electrons: rubber, steel, plastic, dry wood.
items.answer: Conductors: steel; insulators: rubber, plastic, dry wood. Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why repulsion, not attraction, is the only sure test that an object is a magnet. (b) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets.
items.answer: (a) Attraction occurs between a magnet and any magnetic material, so it does not prove the object is a magnet; only a magnet can repel another magnet. (b) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current.

items.stem: The gravitational field strength on Mars is 3.7 N/kg. Calculate the weight of a 80 kg astronaut there.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 80 × 3.7 = 296 N. Mass stays 80 kg.

items.stem: A wire of constant temperature is used in a circuit. The length of the wire is increased by 50% while the cross-sectional area of the wire stays the same. State and explain how the resistance of the wire changes.
items.answer: The resistance of the wire increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using R ∝ L/A: resistance of the wire ∝ length of the wire; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Am-241 (proton number 95) decays by alpha emission to form Np. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Np.
items.answer: Np: nucleon number 237, proton number 93. Am-241 (Z = 95) → Np-237 (Z = 93) + α (He-4, Z = 2)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 237; 1 mark proton number 93; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: Engineers in Nairobi are designing a harbour where incoming ocean waves have a wavelength of about 20 m. Two entrance widths are proposed: 20 m and 120 m. Using ideas about diffraction, evaluate which entrance would give calmer water for boats moored to one side of the entrance.
items.answer: The 120 m entrance: when the gap is much larger than λ the waves diffract little, so less wave energy spreads to the sides. A 20 m gap would spread waves widely into the harbour (though it lets in less energy overall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction greatest when gap ≈ λ; 1 mark: wide gap gives little spreading to the side; 1 mark: balanced point (narrow gap admits less energy but spreads it); 1 mark: clear conclusion.

items.stem: A infrared signal has a frequency of 7.5 × 10¹² Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum (speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).

A documentary follows the life of a star with 30 times the Sun’s mass. (a) Explain why the star is stable during its main-sequence stage. (b) Describe the later stages of the star’s life. (c) Explain why elements formed in stars end up in planets. (d) State the main source of the star’s energy.
items.answer: (a) Outward thermal pressure balances the inward gravitational force. (b) Red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole. (c) Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space; they join later nebulae that form new stars and planets. (d) Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.

items.stem: A science article compares nuclear fission reactors with experimental fusion reactors. (a) Describe nuclear fusion and state where it occurs naturally. (b) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth. (c) State one advantage and one disadvantage of fission power compared with burning fossil fuels.
items.answer: (a) Two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus (helium), releasing energy; in stars. (b) Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei; hard to contain. (c) No CO₂ emitted during generation; produces long-lived radioactive waste.

items.stem: An electric fan contains a d.c. motor powered by a 12 V battery. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (c) Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in keeping rotation continuous.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (c) It reverses the current every half turn so the turning effect stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A 2400 W metal-cased microwave oven is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. (a) Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect the user if the live wire touches the case. (b) Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin. (c) State one advantage of a residual current circuit breaker over a fuse.
items.answer: (a) Large current flows through the low-resistance earth wire, melting the fuse and disconnecting the live supply. (b) A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire. (c) It acts faster and can be reset.

items.stem: A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter, then pulls it out. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (c) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows. (d) Explain why the meter deflects the opposite way when the magnet is pulled out.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (c) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed. (d) The change in field is reversed, so the induced e.m.f. reverses.

items.stem: An archaeologist uses carbon-14 to date a wooden bowl. (a) Explain why the half-life of the source matters for this use. (b) Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination in this context. (c) Explain why ionising radiation can be harmful to living cells.
items.answer: (a) Long half-life for steady count over years; short half-life for medical use so the dose to the patient is low. (b) Irradiation: exposed to radiation from outside, does not become radioactive; contamination: radioactive material gets on/in the object. (c) It ionises molecules, damaging DNA and causing mutation or cell death.

items.stem: Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N/kg. (a) State the force that keeps it in orbit and its direction. (b) Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Earth.
items.answer: (a) Gravitational attraction of the Sun, towards the Sun. (b) 500 s

items.stem: A 9 V battery drives a current of 2.50 A through a lamp for 300 s. (a) Calculate the charge that passes through the device. (b) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (c) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 750 C (b) 6750 J (c) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 600; paper 595; 3 mm aluminium 24; 2 cm lead 21. Background is 18 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A student sets up a ripple tank with a vibrating bar. The water waves have a frequency of 0.500 Hz and a wavelength of 12.0 m. (a) Calculate the speed of the waves. (b) Calculate the time for a wave to travel 90.0 m. (c) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 6.00 m/s (b) 15 s (c) 6.00 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.

items.stem: Amara is researching satellite television and mobile phones, which uses microwaves. (a) State the speed of this radiation in a vacuum. (b) A typical frequency used is 4.8 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength. (c) Explain why this radiation is suitable for this use. (d) Describe one harmful effect of this radiation and one precaution.
items.answer: (a) 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (b) 6.2 × 10⁻² m (c) They pass through the atmosphere and can be focused into narrow beams. (d) internal heating of body cells; limit exposure time/use shielding.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) λ = c/f [2] (c) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (d) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A spectrum of a galaxy shows its absorption lines shifted towards the red end; its speed of recession is 4.4 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Calculate the distance to the galaxy (H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹). (b) Explain how redshift data support the Big Bang theory.
items.answer: (a) 2.0 × 10²⁴ m (b) More distant galaxies recede faster, so the Universe is expanding from an initial point.

items.stem: Compare the nuclei of oxygen-18 and oxygen-16 (proton number 8): give the numbers of protons and neutrons in each and state what they have in common.
items.answer: oxygen-18: 8 p, 10 n; oxygen-16: 8 p, 8 n. Same proton number, so the same element (isotopes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each nucleus; 1 mark isotopes/same Z.

items.stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets, connected through a split-ring commutator. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State two ways to increase the size of the force.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns).

items.stem: A street-light controller uses an LDR in series with a 10 kΩ resistor across a 12 V supply, with the output taken across the LDR. The LDR is 1 kΩ in daylight and 20 kΩ at night. (a) Calculate the output p.d. in daylight and at night. (b) The lamp switches on when the output exceeds 6 V. Explain whether the circuit works as intended.
items.answer: (a) Day: 1.09 V; night: 8.00 V. (b) Yes: 8.00 V > 6 V at night switches the lamp on; 1.09 V < 6 V in daylight keeps it off.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks each using V = 12 × R_LDR/(R_LDR + 10); (b) 1 mark comparison with 6 V, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A phone charger transformer steps 230 V down to 12 V and supplies a current of 2.00 A to the phone. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate the current in the primary coil.

A polythene rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth and becomes negatively charged with a charge of magnitude 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod became charged. (b) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it. (c) Describe the electric field pattern around the rod tip if it acts like a point charge.
items.answer: (a) Electrons moved onto the polythene rod from the cloth. (b) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion. (c) Radial lines pointing inwards.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (c) Explain why aluminium is not attracted. (d) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (c) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it. (d) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why do fusion reactions need extremely high temperatures? (b) Nuclear fission is
items.answer: (a) Nuclei must move fast enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them (b) the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei
items.markingKey: (a) Both nuclei are positive and repel. (b) Fission: U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing energy and 2–3 neutrons.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A voltmeter is connected (b) The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is
items.answer: (a) in parallel across the component (b) the electrical work done by the source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit
items.markingKey: (a) Voltmeters measure the p.d. across a component and have very high resistance. (b) e.m.f. = energy supplied per unit charge by the source (V = W/Q).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets. (b) Explain why an unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to either pole of a magnet.
items.answer: (a) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current. (b) Magnetism is induced in the nail: the end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: induced magnetism; 1 mark: near end opposite pole → attraction.

items.stem: The gravitational field strength on Mercury is 3.7 N/kg. Calculate the weight of a 80 kg astronaut there.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 80 × 3.7 = 296 N. Mass stays 80 kg.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the electric field between two parallel plates, one positive and one negative. (b) Explain why you sometimes get a small shock touching a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet.
items.answer: (a) Uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from the positive plate to the negative plate (curving slightly at the edges). (b) Friction between shoes and carpet charges your body; when you touch the earthed metal handle, charge flows suddenly through you to earth.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: parallel equally spaced; 1 mark: + to −. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 3.00 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 3.60 cm wide and gap B is 15.0 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.
items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spreads (curved); 1 mark: B mainly straight; 1 mark: same wavelength drawn/stated.

items.stem: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi use which type of electromagnetic wave?
items.answer: Microwaves (and short-wavelength radio)
items.markingKey: Wireless networking uses about 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz microwaves.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Light takes about 4.2 years to reach us from the nearest star after the Sun. Its distance is about (b) The Milky Way is
items.answer: (a) 4.2 light-years (b) a galaxy containing billions of stars
items.markingKey: (a) Distance in light-years = years of travel. (b) Our galaxy has 100–400 billion stars.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Compare the a.c. generator and the d.c. motor in terms of energy changes. (b) Explain why slip rings, not a split-ring commutator, are used in an a.c. generator.
items.answer: (a) Generator: kinetic → electrical; motor: electrical → kinetic. (b) Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same brush, so the output alternates.

items.stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets, connected through a split-ring commutator. State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed.
items.answer: The force stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is increased by 50%. State and explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A 17.0 V battery is connected in series with resistors of 5 Ω and 12 Ω. Calculate (a) the total resistance, (b) the current and (c) the p.d. across the 5 Ω resistor.
Answer both parts. (a) A very small number of alpha particles bounced back. What did this show? (b) The proton number (atomic number) of a nucleus is
items.answer: (a) The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (b) the number of protons
items.markingKey: (a) Large deflections need a concentrated positive charge and mass. (b) Z = number of protons; A = protons + neutrons.

items.stem: How does the resistance of a wire change if its length is doubled?
items.answer: It doubles

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe how to demagnetise a steel bar using electricity. (b) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets.
items.answer: (a) Place it in a coil carrying alternating current and slowly pull it out of the coil (or reduce the a.c. to zero). (b) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: a.c. coil; 1 mark: withdraw slowly / reduce current. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Mars orbits the Sun at an average distance of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 687 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.7 N/kg. Calculate the weight of a 90 kg probe on its surface.

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the difference between an electrical conductor and an insulator in terms of electrons. (b) Explain why the charge on a rubbed insulator stays in one place while charge on a conductor spreads out.
items.answer: (a) In conductors, electrons are free to move through the material; in insulators electrons are bound to atoms and cannot move. (b) Electrons cannot move through an insulator, but in a conductor they move freely and repel each other, spreading over the surface.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 2.50 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 3.00 cm wide and gap B is 15.0 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.
items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spreads (curved); 1 mark: B mainly straight; 1 mark: same wavelength drawn/stated.

items.stem: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used for detecting forged banknotes?
items.answer: ultraviolet
items.markingKey: Ultraviolet: it makes fluorescent security ink glow.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a main-sequence star stays stable for billions of years. (b) Explain why elements heavier than iron are thought to form in supernovae.
items.answer: (a) The outward pressure from the hot gas (from fusion energy) balances the inward pull of gravity. (b) Fusion in stars can build elements only up to iron; the huge energy of a supernova explosion makes heavier nuclei, which are scattered into space.

items.stem: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 240 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 24.0 V; step-down

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the two sides of a coil in a motor experience forces in opposite directions. (b) Explain why the coil in a motor is wound on a soft-iron core.
items.answer: (a) The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by Fleming’s left-hand rule the forces are opposite, giving a turning effect. (b) The iron concentrates the magnetic field, increasing the force and turning effect.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 720; paper 720; 3 mm aluminium 30; 2 cm lead 216. Background is 24 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A potential divider has R₁ = 1 kΩ and R₂ = 2 kΩ in series across a 9 V supply. Calculate the output p.d. across R₂.
Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what the notation ²³⁵₉₂U tells you about the nucleus. (b) Explain why two isotopes of the same element have different masses.
items.answer: (a) Nucleon number 235 (protons + neutrons), proton number 92, so 143 neutrons. (b) They have different numbers of neutrons, and each neutron adds mass.

items.stem: A current of 0.100 A passes through a 8 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across it.
Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how iron filings show a magnetic field pattern but do not show its direction. (b) Explain why magnetic field lines never cross.
items.answer: (a) Each filing becomes a tiny induced magnet and lines up with the field, but filings have no marked north end, so the direction is not shown. (b) At any point the field has only one direction; if lines crossed, a compass there would point two ways at once.

items.stem: Mars is 2.28 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun. Calculate how long sunlight takes to reach it, in minutes.
items.answer: 12.7 minutes

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 10.0 Hz. Calculate its period, giving the unit.
State two properties that infrared and microwaves have in common, and one way in which they differ.
items.answer: Both are transverse, travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and can travel through a vacuum (any two). They differ in wavelength/frequency (and energy).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two shared properties (transverse; same speed in vacuum; no medium needed; can be reflected/refracted); 1 mark: different wavelength/frequency.

items.stem: Light from a distant galaxy shows a redshift that corresponds to a recession speed of 1.1 × 10⁶ m/s. Convert the distance to light-years (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m).
items.answer: 5.3 × 10⁷ light-years

items.stem: A bicycle dynamo lights a lamp. The number of turns on the coil is halved while the speed of the magnet stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the induced e.m.f. changes.
items.answer: The induced e.m.f. halves.
items.markingKey: Using induced e.m.f. ∝ rate of change of magnetic field: induced e.m.f. ∝ number of turns on the coil; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: An electric fan contains a d.c. motor powered by a 12 V battery. (a) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed. (b) Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in keeping rotation continuous.
items.answer: (a) The force stays in the same direction. (b) It reverses the current every half turn so the turning effect stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a technetium tracer records a corrected count rate of 3200 counts/min. The background count rate is 25 counts/min and the half-life is 5 hours. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 15 hours. (b) Explain why the count rate fluctuates even though the half-life is constant. (c) State two sources of background radiation.
items.answer: (a) 400 counts/min (b) Radioactive decay is random; the number decaying each second varies. (c) Radon gas from rocks; cosmic rays (or food, buildings, medical).

items.stem: A 2000 W metal-cased hair dryer is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. (a) Calculate the normal working current. (b) Choose a fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and justify the choice. (c) Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin.
items.answer: (a) 8.70 A (b) 13 A (c) A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire.
items.markingKey: (a) I = P/V = 2000/230 [2] (b) just above working current [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Stars such as the Sun release energy in their cores. (a) Explain how a chain reaction is controlled. (b) Describe nuclear fusion and state where it occurs naturally. (c) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth. (d) State one advantage and one disadvantage of fission power compared with burning fossil fuels.
items.answer: (a) Control rods absorb some of the neutrons so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another. (b) Two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus (helium), releasing energy; in stars. (c) Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei; hard to contain. (d) No CO₂ emitted during generation; produces long-lived radioactive waste.

items.stem: A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 60 s. (a) Calculate the power of the device. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery. (c) Calculate the number of electrons passing in 60 s (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.answer: (a) 2.40 W (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit. (c) 7.5 × 10¹⁹

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a technetium tracer records a corrected count rate of 960 counts/min. The background count rate is 40 counts/min and the half-life is 2 minutes. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 4 minutes. (b) Calculate the reading the counter shows after 4 minutes. (c) Describe how to measure the background count rate.
items.answer: (a) 240 counts/min (b) 280 counts/min (c) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute.

items.stem: Venus orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.08 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 225 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 8.9 N/kg. (a) Calculate the weight of a 60 kg probe on its surface. (b) State the force that keeps it in orbit and its direction. (c) Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Venus.
items.answer: (a) 534 N (b) Gravitational attraction of the Sun, towards the Sun. (c) 360 s

items.stem: A balloon is rubbed with a jumper and becomes negatively charged with a charge of magnitude 4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod became charged. (b) Calculate the number of electrons transferred (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (c) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it. (d) Explain why the same experiment does not work with a metal rod held in the hand.
items.answer: (a) Electrons moved onto the balloon from the cloth. (b) 3.0 × 10¹⁰ (c) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion. (d) Charge flows through the conducting metal and the body to earth.

items.stem: A ripple tank vibrator runs at 4 Hz. In the deep region the wavelength is 2.50 cm. The waves cross into a shallow region where their speed falls to 0.0750 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep region. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow region. (c) Explain what happens to the direction of the waves if they meet the boundary at an angle.
items.answer: (a) 0.100 m/s (b) 1.88 cm (c) They refract towards the normal because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 4 × 0.0250 = 0.100 m/s [2]; (b) f unchanged = 4 Hz, λ = 0.0750/4 = 0.0187 m = 1.88 cm [2]; (c) wave slows, bends towards the normal [1].

items.stem: A company uses ultraviolet for sterilising water. (a) Explain why this radiation is suitable for this use. (b) Compare this radiation with infrared, used for remote controls for televisions, in terms of wavelength and frequency.
items.answer: (a) High-energy photons kill bacteria. (b) ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than infrared.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Astronomers measure the speed of a galaxy moving away from the Milky Way as 3.3 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Convert the distance to light-years (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m). (b) Estimate the age of the Universe from H₀ and state an assumption.
items.answer: (a) 1.6 × 10⁸ light-years (b) 1/H₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years; assumes constant expansion rate.

items.stem: A transformer at a substation has a primary voltage of 230 V. The turns ratio Np : Ns is 500 : 40. (a) State whether it is a step-up or step-down transformer. (b) The secondary current is 2.00 A. Calculate the primary current, assuming 100% efficiency. (c) Explain why the transformer would not work with a d.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) step-down (b) 0.160 A (c) A steady current gives a constant field; no change in field so no e.m.f. induced.

items.stem: A beam of electrons enters a region of uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. (a) State the rule used to predict the direction of the force and what each finger represents. (b) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (c) Describe the effect of replacing the d.c. supply with an a.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion. (b) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (c) The force reverses direction many times a second, so the object vibrates (as in a loudspeaker).

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near an iodine source records a corrected count rate of 800 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min and the half-life is 3 hours. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 6 hours. (b) Calculate the reading the counter shows after 6 hours. (c) Describe how to measure the background count rate. (d) State two sources of background radiation.
items.answer: (a) 200 counts/min (b) 220 counts/min (c) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute. (d) Radon gas from rocks; cosmic rays (or food, buildings, medical).

items.stem: Resistors of 10 Ω and 15 Ω are connected in parallel across a 9 V supply. Calculate (a) the current in each resistor, (b) the total current and (c) the combined resistance.
items.markingKey: (a) I = V/R in each branch (full 9 V across each) [2]; (b) sum = 1.50 A [1]; (c) R = V/I = 9/1.50 = 6.00 Ω or 1/R = 1/10 + 1/15 [2].

items.stem: The nuclide strontium-90 has proton number 38. (a) State the number of neutrons in the nucleus. (b) Describe how the alpha-particle scattering experiment showed that the nucleus is small and positive.
items.answer: (a) 52 (b) Most alpha particles passed straight through; a few were deflected through large angles by a small, concentrated positive charge.

items.stem: In a torch, the battery has an e.m.f. of 6 V and the bulb draws 0.400 A. It is switched on for 60 s. (a) Calculate the charge that passes through the device. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 24.0 C (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (b) Explain why aluminium is not attracted. (c) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (b) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it. (c) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls.

items.stem: Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the average orbital speed. (b) Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Earth.
items.markingKey: (a) v = 2πr/T with T in s [3] (b) t = d/c [2]

items.stem: A perspex ruler is rubbed with a silk and becomes positively charged with a charge of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Calculate the number of electrons transferred (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (b) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it. (c) Describe the electric field pattern around the rod tip if it acts like a point charge.
items.answer: (a) 1.0 × 10¹⁰ (b) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion. (c) Radial lines pointing outwards.

items.stem: In a ripple tank the water waves have wavelength 1.50 cm in the deep part. The dipper vibrates at 4 Hz. Over a shallow region the waves move at 0.0480 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) State which quantity does not change as the waves cross into shallow water. (c) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why. (d) The waves then pass through a gap 7.20 cm wide. Describe the diffraction pattern.
items.answer: (a) 0.0600 m/s (b) Frequency (c) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down. (d) Little spreading, mainly straight wavefronts with curved edges (gap ≫ λ).
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 4 × 0.0150 = 0.0600 m/s [2] (b) frequency set by source [1] (c) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2] (d) 1 mark pattern linked to gap/λ; 1 mark wavelength unchanged [2]

items.stem: Which is a harmful effect of excessive exposure to X-rays?
options: no harmful effects at any intensity
mutation or damage to cells, leading to cancer
items.answer: mutation or damage to cells, leading to cancer
items.markingKey: X-rays: mutation or damage to cells, leading to cancer.

items.stem: In a series circuit, the current is
items.answer: the same at every point
items.markingKey: There is only one path, so the same charge per second passes every point.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A chain of iron paper clips hangs from a magnet. Explain what happens when the magnet is removed if the clips are soft iron, and if they are steel. (b) Describe how to demagnetise a steel bar using electricity.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron clips lose their induced magnetism and fall apart; steel clips keep some magnetism and may stay together. (b) Place it in a coil carrying alternating current and slowly pull it out of the coil (or reduce the a.c. to zero).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: a.c. coil; 1 mark: withdraw slowly / reduce current.

items.stem: The gravitational field strength on Venus is 8.9 N/kg. Calculate the weight of a 55 kg astronaut there.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 55 × 8.9 = 490 N. Mass stays 55 kg.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the difference between the plum-pudding model and the nuclear model. (b) Explain why the alpha-scattering experiment had to be done in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) Plum pudding: positive charge spread through the atom with electrons embedded; nuclear: tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons around it, mostly empty space. (b) Alpha particles would be absorbed by air after a few cm, so they would not reach the foil or detector.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 60 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is halved. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 60 Hz (b) frequency becomes 30.0 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is halved as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) When a plane water wave reflects off a straight barrier, which is true? (b) Diffraction is greatest when the gap width is
items.answer: (a) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (b) about the same as the wavelength
items.markingKey: (a) Law of reflection: i = r, measured from the normal; λ and f are unchanged. (b) Spreading is most noticeable when gap ≈ λ.

items.stem: The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is greatest when the wire is
options: at right angles to the field
items.answer: at right angles to the field

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is tripled. State and explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time triples.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A rod gains a charge of −4.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ C when rubbed. The charge on one electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate how many electrons were transferred to the rod.
items.answer: 3.0 × 10⁹ electrons

items.stem: Explain why an appliance rated "2 kW, 230 V" draws a larger current than one rated "1 kW, 230 V".
items.answer: P = IV with V fixed, so I ∝ P; double the power means double the current.

items.stem: An object is 2.3 × 10⁴ light-years away. Calculate its distance in km (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹² km) and explain what we are seeing when we look at it.
items.answer: 2.2 × 10¹⁷ km; light that left it 2.3 × 10⁴ years ago.
items.markingKey: 2 marks distance; 1 mark looking back in time.

items.stem: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used for medical imaging of bones?
items.answer: X-rays
items.markingKey: X-rays: they pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a parallel circuit, the current from the source is (b) Two 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the combined resistance?
items.answer: (a) equal to the sum of the currents in the branches (b) 3 Ω
items.markingKey: (a) Current splits at a junction: I = I₁ + I₂. (b) 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 → R = 3 Ω.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why magnetic field lines never cross. (b) Describe the magnetic field between two north poles placed near each other.
items.answer: (a) At any point the field has only one direction; if lines crossed, a compass there would point two ways at once. (b) Field lines from both poles curve away; there is a neutral point midway where the fields cancel.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: lines repel/curve away; 1 mark: neutral point.

items.stem: Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N/kg. Explain why planets further from the Sun have longer orbital periods.
items.answer: They travel a longer distance per orbit and move more slowly because the Sun’s gravitational field is weaker there.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what the notation ²³⁵₉₂U tells you about the nucleus. (b) Explain why the proton number identifies the element.
items.answer: (a) Nucleon number 235 (protons + neutrons), proton number 92, so 143 neutrons. (b) Each element has a unique number of protons; changing it changes the element.

items.stem: A transformer has 500 primary turns and 4000 secondary turns. The primary is connected to a 230 V a.c. supply. The secondary current is 2.00 A. Calculate the primary current, assuming 100% efficiency.
Answer both parts. (a) What happens to the wavelength of water waves when they diffract through a gap? (b) Why do water waves refract when they enter shallower water?
items.answer: (a) It stays the same (b) Their speed changes
items.markingKey: (a) Diffraction changes the direction/spreading, not the speed, frequency or wavelength. (b) Waves slow down in shallow water; the change of speed at an angle changes direction.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A beam of electrons passes through a magnetic field at right angles. Explain why its path curves. (b) Explain how increasing the current affects the force on a wire in a magnetic field, and why.
items.answer: (a) Moving charges are a current, so each electron feels a force at right angles to its velocity and to the field; this continually changes its direction. (b) The force increases (in proportion to current) because the magnetic field around the wire is stronger, so the interaction is greater.

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 960 Bq. Its half-life is 15 years. Calculate its activity after 45 years.
items.answer: 120 Bq

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why charging by friction cannot produce a positive charge by "adding protons". (b) A student rubs a glass rod with silk and it becomes positive. Explain what has happened to the silk and why.
items.answer: (a) Protons are fixed in the nuclei; only electrons are free to move, so an object becomes positive by losing electrons. (b) The silk gains the electrons lost by the glass, so it becomes equally negatively charged; charge is conserved.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: silk negative; 1 mark: equal and opposite (conservation).

items.stem: A current of 2.50 A flows through a heater element for 15 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 15 × 60 = 900 s; Q = It = 2.50 × 900 = 2250 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: Describe what is happening inside a white dwarf, and state the stage that comes after it for a star of suitable mass.
items.answer: Hot, dense core left after outer layers are shed; no fusion, slowly cooling.
items.markingKey: 2 marks description; 1 mark correct neighbouring stage.

items.stem: State two properties that infrared and visible light have in common, and one way in which they differ.
items.answer: Both are transverse, travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and can travel through a vacuum (any two). They differ in wavelength/frequency (and energy).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two shared properties (transverse; same speed in vacuum; no medium needed; can be reflected/refracted); 1 mark: different wavelength/frequency.

items.stem: A 700 W metal-cased heater is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin.
items.answer: A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why asteroids are classed as minor planets. (b) Explain why a comet’s speed changes during its elliptical orbit.
items.answer: (a) They are small rocky bodies orbiting the Sun that have not cleared their orbit and are not massive enough to be planets. (b) Close to the Sun the gravitational pull is stronger and it gains kinetic energy as it falls in; it slows as it moves away.

items.stem: In a reactor, each fission releases on average 2.6 neutrons. Explain what fraction of these must, on average, go on to cause another fission for steady power, and how the moderator affects the reactor.
items.answer: Exactly one neutron per fission must cause another (the rest are absorbed or escape). Control rods absorb neutrons to set this rate; the moderator slows neutrons so they cause fission; the coolant removes heat to the boiler.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one per fission; 1 mark: role of named component.

items.stem: A bicycle dynamo has a magnet that spins inside a coil 5 times per second. State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f.
items.answer: Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two).

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 2 Hz and wave Q has frequency 20 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave P (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 100 turns and carries 1.0 A; electromagnet Y has 200 turns and carries 0.5 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: Both equal – strength depends on turns × current (100 for X, 100 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the count rate measured near a source should be corrected for background radiation. (b) Explain why a Geiger counter detects alpha particles only if it is very close to the source.
items.answer: (a) Background radiation is always present and adds to the counts; it must be measured without the source and subtracted to get the count rate from the source alone. (b) Alpha particles travel only a few cm in air before losing their energy.

items.stem: The p.d. across a lamp is 30.0 V and the current is 2.00 A. Calculate its resistance.

A spectrum of a galaxy shows its absorption lines shifted towards the red end; its speed of recession is 3.3 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Convert the distance to light-years (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m). (b) State one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang. (c) Estimate the age of the Universe from H₀ and state an assumption.
items.answer: (a) 1.6 × 10⁸ light-years (b) Cosmic microwave background radiation. (c) 1/H₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years; assumes constant expansion rate.

items.stem: Food is passed through a beam of gamma radiation before packaging. (a) State which type of radiation is suitable and explain why. (b) Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination in this context. (c) Explain why ionising radiation can be harmful to living cells.
items.answer: (a) Depends on penetration: alpha for short-range ionisation, beta for thin sheet thickness, gamma to pass through the body or packaging. (b) Irradiation: exposed to radiation from outside, does not become radioactive; contamination: radioactive material gets on/in the object. (c) It ionises molecules, damaging DNA and causing mutation or cell death.

items.stem: A report describes how visible light are used for photography and vision. (a) A typical frequency used is 1.4 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Calculate its wavelength. (b) Explain why this radiation is suitable for this use. (c) Compare this radiation with X-rays, used for airport security scanners, in terms of wavelength and frequency. (d) Explain why this radiation is considered low-risk at normal intensities.
items.answer: (a) 2.2 × 10⁻⁷ m (b) It is detected by the eye and by camera sensors. (c) visible light has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than X-rays. (d) It is low frequency and non-ionising; at low intensity it causes no significant heating.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = c/f [2] (b) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) [2]

items.stem: Zara builds a circuit with a 9 V supply: a 2 Ω resistor, then a junction leading to 4 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in parallel. (a) Calculate the total resistance of the circuit. (b) Calculate the p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor. (c) The 4 Ω resistor is removed. State and explain what happens to the battery current. (d) Calculate the power dissipated in the whole circuit.
items.answer: (a) 4.00 Ω (b) 4.50 V (c) It decreases: total resistance increases (only one path through the parallel section). (d) 20.2 W

items.stem: A scrap-yard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars. (a) State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger. (b) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off. (c) Suggest why the device could fail if the coil were wound on a steel core.
items.answer: (a) More turns; larger current (or soft-iron core). (b) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls. (c) Steel keeps its magnetism, so the object would stay attracted after switching off.

items.stem: Mercury orbits the Sun at an average distance of 5.80 × 10¹⁰ m with a period of 88 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.7 N/kg. (a) Calculate the weight of a 50 kg probe on its surface. (b) Explain why planets further from the Sun have longer orbital periods. (c) Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Mercury.
items.answer: (a) 185 N (b) They travel a longer distance per orbit and move more slowly because the Sun’s gravitational field is weaker there. (c) 193 s

items.stem: The nuclide potassium-40 has proton number 19. (a) Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties. (b) Describe how the alpha-particle scattering experiment showed that the nucleus is small and positive. (c) State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
items.answer: (a) Same number of protons and electrons; chemistry depends on electrons. (b) Most alpha particles passed straight through; a few were deflected through large angles by a small, concentrated positive charge. (c) proton +1, 1; neutron 0, 1; electron −1, about 1/1840

items.stem: An engineer tests a transformer: primary 230 V a.c., 800 turns; secondary 100 turns. (a) State whether it is a step-up or step-down transformer. (b) Explain how an e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil. (c) Explain why the core is made of soft iron.
