items.answer: (a) step-down (b) Alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which links the secondary and induces an e.m.f. (c) It is easily magnetised and demagnetised, concentrating the changing field to link both coils.

items.stem: A model harbour is built in a ripple tank. Waves are produced at 4 Hz with wavelength 2.50 cm in deep water and slow to 0.0500 m/s near the model beach. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow water.

A loudspeaker contains a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in the field of a permanent magnet. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (c) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (c) The force stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 850; paper 850; 3 mm aluminium 20; 2 cm lead 21. Background is 18 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A balloon is rubbed with a jumper and becomes negatively charged with a charge of magnitude 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod became charged. (b) Explain why the same experiment does not work with a metal rod held in the hand. (c) Describe the electric field pattern around the rod tip if it acts like a point charge.
items.answer: (a) Electrons moved onto the balloon from the cloth. (b) Charge flows through the conducting metal and the body to earth. (c) Radial lines pointing inwards.

items.stem: A 6 V battery drives a current of 2.50 A through a lamp for 120 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the device when working. (c) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery. (d) Calculate the number of electrons passing in 120 s (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.answer: (a) 1800 J (b) 2.40 Ω (c) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit. (d) 1.9 × 10²¹

items.stem: Galaxy data (distance / million light-years; recession speed / m/s): E: 400, 8.8 × 10⁶; B: 120, 2.6 × 10⁶; D: 310, 6.8 × 10⁶. Describe the relationship and explain what it suggests about the Universe.
items.answer: Speed is (roughly) directly proportional to distance: further galaxies recede faster. This suggests the Universe is expanding, consistent with the Big Bang.
items.markingKey: 1 mark proportional/positive correlation; 1 mark expansion; 1 mark Big Bang link.

items.stem: A radio signal has a frequency of 6.0 × 10⁵ Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum (speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
A potential divider has R₁ = 5 kΩ and R₂ = 10 kΩ in series across a 12 V supply. Calculate the output p.d. across R₂.

A recycling plant separates steel cans from aluminium cans on a conveyor belt. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (c) Explain why aluminium is not attracted.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (c) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it.

items.stem: Mercury orbits the Sun at an average distance of 5.80 × 10¹⁰ m with a period of 88 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.7 N/kg. (a) Explain why planets further from the Sun have longer orbital periods. (b) Describe how the accretion model explains the formation of the planets.
items.answer: (a) They travel a longer distance per orbit and move more slowly because the Sun’s gravitational field is weaker there. (b) A rotating disc of gas and dust around the young Sun; particles collided and clumped by gravity into planets; rocky near the Sun, gaseous further out.

items.stem: A nucleus of cobalt (Co) has nucleon number 60 and proton number 27. (a) State the number of neutrons in the nucleus. (b) Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties. (c) State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
items.answer: (a) 33 (b) Same number of protons and electrons; chemistry depends on electrons. (c) proton +1, 1; neutron 0, 1; electron −1, about 1/1840

items.stem: A small wind turbine drives a coil that rotates 10 times per second in a magnetic field. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (c) State the frequency of the a.c. output. (d) Describe how the output voltage–time graph changes if the speed doubles.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (c) 10 Hz (d) Peaks twice as high and twice as many cycles per second.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The direction of an electric field at a point is the direction of the force on (b) Why are aircraft earthed before refuelling?
items.answer: (a) a small positive charge placed there (b) To stop charge building up and causing a spark that ignites fuel vapour
items.markingKey: (a) Field direction = direction of force on a positive test charge. (b) Fuel flowing through the hose can charge the aircraft; earthing lets charge flow safely away.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) An e.m.f. is induced in a wire when (b) The direction of an induced current is always such that it
items.answer: (a) the wire cuts magnetic field lines (b) opposes the change producing it
items.markingKey: (a) Induction needs relative movement or a changing field linked to the conductor. (b) Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change that causes it.

items.stem: Explain why infrared is suitable for optical fibres for broadband.
items.answer: It travels along glass fibres by total internal reflection with little absorption.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property (it travels along glass fibres by total internal reflection with little absorption); 1 mark: linked to the use.

items.stem: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf main-sequence star. State the stage of its life cycle it has reached and predict what will happen to it next, giving a reason.
items.answer: Red dwarf main-sequence star; next: very long main-sequence life, then white dwarf, because its fate depends on its mass.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stage; 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (mass).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how alpha, beta and gamma radiation are deflected differently in an electric field. (b) Explain why radon gas is a significant source of background radiation in some homes.
items.answer: (a) α (positive) deflects towards the negative plate, β (negative) deflects more strongly towards the positive plate as it is much lighter, γ is undeflected (no charge). (b) Radon from granite rock seeps into buildings; it is breathed in and emits alpha particles inside the lungs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each for α, β, γ. (b) [2]

items.stem: Resistors of 10 Ω and 15 Ω are connected in parallel across a 24 V supply. Calculate (a) the current in each resistor, (b) the total current and (c) the combined resistance.
items.markingKey: (a) I = V/R in each branch (full 24 V across each) [2]; (b) sum = 4.00 A [1]; (c) R = V/I = 24/4.00 = 6.00 Ω or 1/R = 1/10 + 1/15 [2].

items.stem: Name the part of a d.c. motor that reverses the current every half turn.
items.answer: Split-ring commutator

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which material is best for making a permanent magnet? (b) Which of these metals is magnetic?
items.answer: (a) Steel (b) Nickel
items.markingKey: (a) Steel is hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism. (b) Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; aluminium, copper and brass are not.

items.stem: Explain why the p.d.s across two lamps in series add up to the e.m.f. of the cell.
items.answer: Energy given to each coulomb by the cell equals the energy transferred by it in the lamps (conservation of energy).

items.stem: Jupiter orbits the Sun at an average distance of 7.78 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 4333 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 24.8 N/kg. State the force that keeps it in orbit and its direction.
items.answer: Gravitational attraction of the Sun, towards the Sun.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 2 Hz and wave Q has frequency 10 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave P (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: The nuclide carbon-14 is written as C with nucleon number 14 and proton number 6. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.
items.answer: 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 6; neutrons = A − Z = 8; electrons = protons in neutral atom = 6.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why do metals conduct electricity? (b) Why is the outer layer of an electric cable made of PVC?
items.answer: (a) They contain free electrons that can move through the metal (b) PVC is an insulator, so it stops charge flowing to the user
items.markingKey: (a) Delocalised electrons carry charge. (b) Insulators prevent current reaching people.

items.stem: Doubling the current in a transmission line makes the power lost
items.answer: four times bigger

items.stem: State two properties that microwaves and radio waves have in common, and one way in which they differ.

items.answer: (a) 3.0 × 10⁰ m (b) Long wavelength diffracts around hills and buildings and reflects off the ionosphere for long-distance broadcasting. (c) It is low frequency and non-ionising; at low intensity it causes no significant heating.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = c/f [2] (b) 1 mark property; 1 mark link [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: A student investigates a heating element connected to a power supply. The resistance is reduced to a quarter while the current stays the same. Explain how the power dissipated in the resistor changes.
items.answer: The power dissipated in the resistor becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power dissipated in the resistor ∝ resistance; factor = 0.250 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Engineers in Lima are designing a harbour where incoming ocean waves have a wavelength of about 8 m. Two entrance widths are proposed: 8 m and 48 m. Using ideas about diffraction, evaluate which entrance would give calmer water for boats moored to one side of the entrance.
items.answer: The 48 m entrance: when the gap is much larger than λ the waves diffract little, so less wave energy spreads to the sides. A 8 m gap would spread waves widely into the harbour (though it lets in less energy overall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction greatest when gap ≈ λ; 1 mark: wide gap gives little spreading to the side; 1 mark: balanced point (narrow gap admits less energy but spreads it); 1 mark: clear conclusion.

items.stem: Diego is studying the isotope potassium-40 (Z = 19). (a) State the number of electrons in a neutral atom. (b) Another isotope of potassium has two more neutrons. State its nucleon number and proton number. (c) State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
items.answer: (a) 19 (b) 42; 19 (c) proton +1, 1; neutron 0, 1; electron −1, about 1/1840

items.stem: Classify these materials as conductors or insulators and explain the difference in terms of electrons: graphite, aluminium, copper, glass.
items.answer: Conductors: graphite, aluminium, copper; insulators: glass. Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not.

items.stem: Light from a distant galaxy shows a redshift that corresponds to a recession speed of 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Explain how redshift data support the Big Bang theory. (b) Estimate the age of the Universe from H₀ and state an assumption.
items.answer: (a) More distant galaxies recede faster, so the Universe is expanding from an initial point. (b) 1/H₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years; assumes constant expansion rate.

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 300 turns and carries 1.0 A; electromagnet Y has 100 turns and carries 0.5 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: X – strength depends on turns × current (300 for X, 50 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: A bicycle dynamo has a magnet that spins inside a coil 25 times per second. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (c) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (c) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed.

items.stem: Mars orbits the Sun at an average distance of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 687 Earth days. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.7 N/kg. (a) Calculate the weight of a 50 kg probe on its surface. (b) State the force that keeps it in orbit and its direction. (c) Describe how the accretion model explains the formation of the planets.
items.answer: (a) 185 N (b) Gravitational attraction of the Sun, towards the Sun. (c) A rotating disc of gas and dust around the young Sun; particles collided and clumped by gravity into planets; rocky near the Sun, gaseous further out.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S.

items.stem: A 700 W metal-cased hair dryer is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. (a) Calculate the normal working current. (b) Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin.
items.answer: (a) 3.04 A (b) A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near an iodine source records a corrected count rate of 2400 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min and the half-life is 5 days. (a) Describe how to measure the background count rate. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 135 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute. (b) Just over 20 days (4 half-lives)

items.stem: A company uses radio waves for radio and television transmissions. (a) State the speed of this radiation in a vacuum. (b) A typical frequency used is 2.0 × 10⁸ Hz. Calculate its wavelength. (c) Explain why this radiation is considered low-risk at normal intensities.
items.answer: (a) 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (b) 1.5 × 10⁰ m (c) It is low frequency and non-ionising; at low intensity it causes no significant heating.

items.stem: A current of 4.00 A flows through a heater element for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 2 × 60 = 120 s; Q = It = 4.00 × 120 = 480 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: A ripple tank vibrator runs at 12 Hz. In the deep region the wavelength is 2.00 cm. The waves cross into a shallow region where their speed falls to 0.144 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep region. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow region. (c) Explain what happens to the direction of the waves if they meet the boundary at an angle.
items.answer: (a) 0.240 m/s (b) 1.20 cm (c) They refract towards the normal because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 12 × 0.0200 = 0.240 m/s [2]; (b) f unchanged = 12 Hz, λ = 0.144/12 = 0.0120 m = 1.20 cm [2]; (c) wave slows, bends towards the normal [1].

items.stem: A nuclear power station uses uranium-235 as fuel. (a) Describe what happens when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission. (b) Explain how a chain reaction is controlled. (c) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth.
items.answer: (a) It absorbs a neutron, becomes unstable and splits into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing 2–3 neutrons and energy. (b) Control rods absorb some of the neutrons so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another. (c) Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei; hard to contain.
